newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan military given formal advisory role.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan military given formal advisory role.

text.p: Pakistani President Farooq Leghari issued a decree on Monday giving the heads of the armed forces a formal advisory role in government affairs with less than a month remaining until national elections.
A top minister denied the move gave the military a formal share in power, saying the council would not undercut parliament or cabinet but only "give mature advice".
"It is no supra-constitution, no supra-cabinet and no supra-government body," Information and Media Development Minister Irshad Ahmad Haqqani told a news conference.
The cabinet of the president's hand-picked caretaker Prime Minister Meraj Khalid unanimously approved the presidential order to form a 10-member Council for Defence and National Security.
The military will have four seats on the council for the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee and chiefs of the army, navy and air force.
The other six seats will be filled by the president as chairman of the council, the prime minister and the ministers for defence, foreign, interior and finance.

There was no immediate reaction by major political parties to the move, the latest in a series of political changes since Leghari sacked prime minister Benazir Bhutto's three-year-old government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, dissolved the National Assembly (lower house) and ordered fresh elections for February 3.
A similar move by late military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq in the 1980s was widely opposed and later abandoned by him.

Monday's decree came only two days after Leghari and Khalid made contradictory statements to journalists -- the president saying the idea was under consideration and the prime minister denying such a move was being planned.

Haqqani denied that the president and the prime minister differed on the issue and said "everbody agreed" with the presidential decree in the cabinet meeting. "This is a unanimous decision of the cabinet."

But political sources said it will be hard for a government to disregard the advice of the military, which has ruled Pakistan for nearly half of the country's existence after the partition of the Indian sub-continent on independence from Britain in 1947.

The subjects on which the council can advise include "determination of national strategy and fixation of priorities in terms of overall national security", formation of a defence policy and coordinating it with external and domestic policies.

It can also be asked to advise the government on "definition of the task of the armed forces...in accordance with the national strategy", economic and financial policies affecting defence and national security, and advise on internal security and proclamation of an emergency.
"Pushing forward the idea of a national security council looks too much of a vote of no-confidence in democratic institutions...," Pakistan's prestigious daily Dawn said in an editorial on Monday.

"Notwithstanding the need for a better system of checks and balances, this does not augur well for a parliamentary form of government...," another daily newspaper, The Nation, said. "Does all this mean that the parliament does not really matter?"
